l: unmarried and widows, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Paul says it is good for the unmarried and widows to remain as he is, but if they lack self-control they should marry. The unmarried care about the things of the Lord, and Paul says he wants to spare them the troubles of marriage.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: The Corinthian believers are instructed to remain in the condition in which they were called, and not to become bondservants of men since they were bought with a price. They are told the time is short, and are urged to live free from cares and to attend to the Lord without distraction.

l: celibacy and self-control, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Paul considers it good not to touch a woman and better to stay unmarried, and he says each person has his own gift from God. Those without self-control should marry, and couples who abstain for a season by consent do so for prayer, lest Satan tempt them through lack of self-control. Paul calls this advice a concession and judgment, not a commandment.

l: calling, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Each person is to walk as God has called him and stay in the calling in which he was called, whether circumcised or uncircumcised, bondservant or free. Circumcision and uncircumcision are nothing compared with keeping God's commandments. A bondservant may take an opportunity to become free, and Paul states that this rule applies in all the assemblies.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Chapter 8 addresses the question of eating things sacrificed to idols. The writer says that those with knowledge know no idol is anything and that there is one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, but warns that knowledge puffs up while love builds up. Not everyone has this knowledge: some with a conscience about idols eat as if the food were sacrificed to an idol, and their weak conscience is defiled. Those with knowledge are told to take care that their liberty does not become a stumbling block, since a weak brother for whom Christ died may perish. The writer concludes that sinning against the brothers is sinning against Christ, and that he himself will eat no meat forever if food causes his brother to stumble.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: God is described as the one God, the Father, of whom are all things and for whom believers live. Anyone who loves God is known by him, and no other God exists beside him.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Jesus Christ is named as the one Lord, through whom are all things and through whom believers live. Christ died for the weak brother, and sinning against the brothers by wounding their conscience is sinning against him.

l: things sacrificed to idols, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Eating things sacrificed to idols is the topic of the chapter. Food in itself does not commend anyone to God, since not eating makes one no worse and eating makes one no better, yet some eat it as a thing sacrificed to an idol and are defiled in conscience, and others may be emboldened to eat it.

l: idols, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Idols are said to be nothing in the world. Although many so-called gods and lords exist in heaven and on earth, believers have only one God and one Lord. Some people, with consciousness of an idol until now, still treat the food as belonging to an idol, and an idol's temple is the place where a person with knowledge might be seen sitting.

l: knowledge, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Knowledge is said to puff up, while love builds up. Anyone who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought, and this knowledge is not in everyone. A weak brother can perish through the knowledge of another.

l: the weak (weak believers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: The weak lack the knowledge about idols, and their conscience is defiled when they eat as of a thing sacrificed to an idol. They can be emboldened to eat by seeing someone with knowledge in an idol's temple and may perish as a result, though each is a brother for whom Christ died.

l: those with knowledge (the strong), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Those with knowledge know that no idol is anything and that there is one God. They are warned that their liberty must not become a stumbling block to the weak, and that wounding a weak conscience is sinning against Christ. The writer models the right response by resolving to eat no meat forever rather than cause a brother to stumble.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: In this chapter the speaker, who is Paul, defends his apostleship to the Corinthian believers, calling them the seal of it, and argues that apostles have a right to eat, drink, take a believing wife, and be supported by their work. He supports this right with examples of soldiers, vineyard planters and shepherds, the law's command not to muzzle an ox, temple servants, and the Lord's ordinance that those who proclaim the Good News should live from it. Paul says he has not used this right so as not to hinder the Good News, and that he preaches under necessity and offers it without charge. He explains that he made himself a servant to all, becoming like Jews, those under the law, those without law, and the weak, in order to gain and save some. He closes with the image of runners in a race and athletes who exercise self-control, saying he runs with purpose and disciplines his body so he will not be disqualified after preaching to others.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Paul defends his apostleship, citing that he has seen Jesus Christ and that the Corinthians are his work in the Lord. He holds that he has the right to financial support but has not used it, preaching under necessity and becoming all things to all people to save some. He disciplines his body like an athlete so he will not be disqualified after preaching to others.

l: Corinthian believers (the readers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: The Corinthians are called the seal of Paul's apostleship in the Lord and his work in the Lord. Paul argues that having sowed spiritual things among them, it is no great matter to reap material support from them, and he points out that others partake of this right over them. He urges them to run the race so as to win.

l: Good News, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: The Good News is what Paul preaches under necessity, and he says the Lord ordained that those who proclaim it should live from it. Paul declines support so as to cause no hindrance to it and presents it without charge. He does all things for its sake, so that he may be a joint partaker of it.

l: apostolic right to financial support, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Paul argues that apostles have the right to eat and drink, to take a believing wife, and to refrain from other work, supported by the examples of soldiers, vineyard planters, shepherds, the ox in the law of Moses, and temple servants. He says the Lord ordained that proclaimers of the Good News live from it. Paul says he and Barnabas nevertheless did not use this right, and that he is not writing to ask for it in his own case.

l: race and athletic games, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Paul uses the race as an image: all run but one receives the prize, and he urges the readers to run so as to win. Athletes exercise self-control for a corruptible crown, whereas believers seek an incorruptible one. Paul says he runs not aimlessly and does not beat the air, but beats his body into submission lest he be disqualified.

l: Paul's preaching without charge, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Paul says his reward is presenting the Good News of Christ without charge, so as not to abuse his authority in it. He would rather die than have anyone make his boasting void, and he says he has used none of his rights. He bears all things so as to cause no hindrance to the Good News.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: The speaker addresses the brothers, recalling that the fathers were all under the cloud, passed through the sea, were baptized into Moses, and shared spiritual food and drink from a rock that was Christ, yet God was displeased with most of them and they were overthrown in the wilderness. Their idolatry, sexual immorality, testing of Christ, and grumbling, each followed by death, are presented as examples and admonitions for those on whom the ends of the ages have come. The speaker assures them that no temptation is beyond what is common to man, that God is faithful and provides a way of escape, and he urges them to flee idolatry. He contrasts the cup and bread of the Lord, a sharing in Christ's blood and body, with sacrifices to demons, saying they cannot partake of both tables. He closes with guidance on eating food in the butcher shop or at an unbeliever's meal, giving up one's liberty for the sake of another's conscience, and doing all to the glory of God without causing stumbling.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Christ is identified as the spiritual rock that followed the fathers in the wilderness, and some of them tested him and perished by serpents. The cup and bread of the Lord's table are described as a sharing of his blood and body.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: God was not well pleased with most of the fathers, who were overthrown in the wilderness. He is described as faithful, not allowing believers to be tempted beyond what they can bear and providing a way of escape. Believers are told to do all to his glory.

l: our fathers (Israelites in the wilderness), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: The fathers were all under the cloud, passed through the sea, were baptized into Moses, and ate and drank spiritual food and drink. Most of them displeased God and fell through lust, idolatry, sexual immorality (twenty-three thousand in one day), testing Christ (serpents), and grumbling (the destroyer). Their experiences are given as examples and admonitions.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: The brothers are told not to be ignorant of the fathers' history and to take it as an example. They are warned to be careful lest they fall, to flee idolatry, to avoid fellowship with demons, and to seek their neighbor's good. They are also instructed on how to eat food in the butcher shop and at an unbeliever's meal.

l: idolatry, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Idolatry is cited as a sin of some of the fathers, who sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play. The brothers are told to flee from it. The speaker says an idol or a thing sacrificed to idols is nothing in itself, yet the sacrifices are made to demons.

l: demons, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: The Gentiles' sacrifices are said to be offered to demons and not to God. The speaker does not want the brothers to have fellowship with demons and says they cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons, or partake of both tables.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: The speaker addresses the brothers as wise men and asks them to judge what he says. He explains that he sets aside his own liberty for others' conscience and seeks not his own profit but the profit of the many, that they may be saved, pleasing all men in all things.

l: temptation, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Temptation is said to be common to man, and God will not allow believers to be tempted above what they are able. He will provide a way of escape so they can endure it. The fathers' lusting is given as an example of yielding to evil desires.

l: Lord's Supper, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: The cup of blessing is called a sharing of the blood of Christ, and the broken bread a sharing of his body. Because there is one loaf, the many who partake are one body. Partaking of the Lord's table excludes partaking of the table of demons.

l: conscience, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Conscience is the basis for eating without questions what is sold in the butcher shop or set before one at an unbeliever's meal. If someone says the food was offered to idols, one should not eat it for the sake of that person's conscience, not one's own. The speaker asks why his liberty should be judged by another's conscience.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: The writer urges the brothers to imitate him as he imitates Christ, praises them for keeping the traditions, and then addresses two problems in their gatherings. First he sets out an order of headship (God, Christ, man, woman) and instructs that a man praying or prophesying should not have his head covered while a woman should be covered, appealing to creation, the angels, nature, and the custom of God's assemblies, while noting that man and woman are interdependent in the Lord. Second, he rebukes the Corinthians because their assemblies bring divisions and because their meal is not the Lord's supper, as some go hungry while others are drunken. He recalls the tradition he received from the Lord about the bread and cup on the night Jesus was betrayed, warns that eating and drinking unworthily brings guilt and judgment (shown in weakness, sickness, and death among them), and tells them to examine themselves, wait for one another, and eat at home if hungry.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Christ is the model Paul imitates, and is described as the head of every man, with God as his head. The text also recounts that the Lord Jesus, on the night he was betrayed, took bread and the cup and gave the words of the new covenant in his blood.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: God is named as the head of Christ, and man is called his image and glory. All things are said to be from God, and the assemblies of God are said to share the custom Paul describes.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Paul urges the brothers to imitate him as he imitates Christ, praises them for remembering him and holding the traditions, and then corrects them on head coverings and the Lord's supper. He says he received the account of the supper from the Lord and delivered it to them, and that he will set the remaining matters in order when he comes.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: The Corinthian believers are praised for remembering Paul and holding the traditions, but not praised for how they gather, since divisions exist among them and their meetings are for the worse. They are told to examine themselves, to wait for one another when they eat, and to eat at home if hungry, with the warning that many among them are weak, sickly, or have died.

l: man, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Man is described as the head of the woman, with Christ as his head, and as the image and glory of God. A man who prays or prophesies with his head covered dishonors his head, and long hair is called a dishonor to him; yet he is not independent of the woman, and he comes through a woman.

l: woman, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Woman is described as the glory of man, made from man and for man, and is told to be covered when praying or prophesying, since being uncovered is likened to being shaved. She is said to have authority over her own head because of the angels, to be not independent of man in the Lord, and to have long hair as a glory and a covering given to her.

l: head covering, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: A head covering is required of a woman who prays or prophesies and forbidden to a man doing the same. Paul supports this with arguments from headship, creation, the angels, nature, and the practice of God's assemblies, and treats it as a matter of honor and shame.

l: Lord's Supper, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Paul says the Corinthians' meal is not the Lord's supper, because each eats his own supper first, so one is hungry and another drunken. He recalls the Lord's bread and cup as a memorial that proclaims the Lord's death until he comes, and warns that eating or drinking unworthily without discerning the Lord's body brings guilt and judgment.

l: assembly of God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: The Corinthian gathering is marked by divisions and factions and is said to be for the worse rather than the better. Paul faults them for despising God's assembly and shaming those who have little, and instructs them to wait for one another so that their coming together is not for judgment.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Addressing the brothers about spiritual things, the writer reminds them that they were once led astray to mute idols and that only the Holy Spirit enables anyone to say "Jesus is Lord." He explains that there are various gifts, services and workings, all from the same Spirit, Lord and God, and that the Spirit gives each person a manifestation for the profit of all, including wisdom, knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, languages and interpretation. He compares Christ and the church to a body with many members, all baptized into one Spirit, whether Jews or Greeks, bond or free. God arranged the members as he desired, so no member can say it has no need of another, and weaker or less honorable members receive more honor so that members care for one another and share suffering and honor. The chapter closes by listing the roles God set in the assembly, noting that not all have the same gift, and urging earnest desire for the best gifts while promising to show a most excellent way.

l: Holy Spirit, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: No one can say "Jesus is Lord" except by the Holy Spirit, and no one speaking by God's Spirit calls Jesus accursed. The same Spirit is the source of all the varied gifts and distributes them to each person separately as he desires. All were baptized in one Spirit into one body and given to drink into one Spirit.

l: Jesus, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Jesus is named in the test of speaking by God's Spirit: no one speaking by the Spirit says "Jesus is accursed." Saying "Jesus is Lord" is possible only by the Holy Spirit.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Christ is likened to a body that is one yet has many members. The believers addressed are said to be the body of Christ, and members individually.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: God is the same God who works all things in all, behind the various kinds of workings. He set each member in the body as he desired and composed the body together, giving more abundant honor to the inferior part so there would be no division. He also set in the assembly apostles, prophets, teachers, miracle workers, healings, helps, governments and various languages.

l: spiritual gifts, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Gifts come in various kinds, with the same Spirit behind them, and each person receives a manifestation of the Spirit for the profit of all. They include the word of wisdom, word of knowledge, faith, healings, miracles, prophecy, discerning of spirits, languages and interpretation. Not all have the same gifts, and the readers are urged to earnestly desire the best gifts, with a most excellent way yet to be shown.

l: body (church as body of Christ), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: The body is one yet has many members, and all who were baptized in one Spirit, Jews or Greeks, bond or free, form it. It is not a single member but many, and God composed it so there is no division and the members care for one another. When one member suffers all suffer, and when one is honored all rejoice.

l: members of the body, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Members such as the foot, ear, eye, hand and head each have their place, and none can claim not to belong because it differs from another, nor say it has no need of another. Members that seem weaker are necessary, and less honorable or unpresentable parts receive more abundant honor and modesty. They are the individual believers, set by God as he desired in roles such as apostles, prophets and teachers, and not all hold the same role.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: The brothers are told the writer does not want them ignorant about spiritual things, and are reminded that as heathen they were led away to mute idols. They are called the body of Christ and members individually. They are urged to earnestly desire the best gifts and promised a most excellent way.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: Chapter 13 describes the supreme importance of love. The speaker says that without love, even speaking in the languages of men and angels, prophecy, all knowledge, mountain-moving faith, giving away goods to the poor, and giving his body to be burned amount to nothing. He then lists the qualities of love: it is patient and kind, bears, believes, hopes, and endures all things, and never fails, while prophecies, languages, and knowledge will be done away with because they are partial. The speaker contrasts his childhood with adulthood and now seeing dimly in a mirror with one day seeing face to face and knowing fully. He concludes that faith, hope, and love remain, and that love is the greatest of the three.

l: love, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: Love is presented as what gives value to every gift and sacrifice; without it, the speaker is nothing and gains no profit. It is described as patient, kind, not envious, not boastful, not proud, not self-seeking, not easily provoked, keeping no account of evil, rejoicing with the truth, and bearing, believing, hoping, and enduring all things. Love never fails, remains when prophecy, languages, and knowledge pass away, and is named the greatest of faith, hope, and love.

l: faith, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: Faith is mentioned as being able to remove mountains, but the speaker says that having all such faith without love leaves him nothing. At the end it is listed with hope and love as one of three things that remain. It is ranked below love, which is the greatest.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: The speaker uses himself as an example, saying that without love his eloquence, prophecy, knowledge, faith, charity, and self-sacrifice would count for nothing, making him like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. He says he knows and prophesies only in part, recalls speaking, feeling, and thinking as a child before putting away childish things as a man, and says he now sees dimly but will one day know fully, as he is fully known.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: In this chapter the writer urges the believers to pursue love and desire spiritual gifts, especially prophesying, because it edifies the assembly while speaking in another language edifies only the speaker unless it is interpreted. He uses the examples of pipe, harp, trumpet, and foreign languages to show that unintelligible speech profits no one, and he says he would rather speak five words with understanding than ten thousand in another language. He explains that other languages are a sign to unbelievers and prophesying a sign to believers, and that an unbeliever who comes in would think the assembly crazy if all spoke in languages, but would be convicted and worship God if all prophesied. He sets rules for gatherings: two or three speak in languages in turn with an interpreter, two or three prophets speak while others discern, and those without an interpreter stay silent. He also tells wives to be quiet in the assemblies, insists his words are the Lord's commandment, and closes by saying all things should be done decently and in order.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: God is the one to whom a person speaking in another language speaks, since no one else understands. He is not a God of confusion but of peace, and an unbeliever convicted by prophecy falls on his face and declares that God is among the assembly.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: Paul urges the believers to pursue love and desire to prophesy, and says he thanks God that he speaks with other languages more than all of them. He says he would rather speak five words with understanding in the assembly than ten thousand in another language, and he claims that what he writes is the commandment of the Lord.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: The brothers are told to seek to abound in building up the assembly, to be mature in thought and babies in malice, and to desire earnestly to prophesy without forbidding other languages. They are given instructions for orderly gatherings, and are asked whether the word of God went out from them or came to them alone.

l: assembly of God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: The assembly is what gifts are meant to build up, and each person who comes together brings a psalm, teaching, revelation, language, or interpretation. Unlearned or unbelieving visitors would call it crazy if all spoke in languages, but would be reproved, have their heart's secrets revealed, and worship God if all prophesied.

l: speaking in other languages, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: Speaking in another language is described as speaking mysteries to God in the Spirit and edifying only oneself unless it is interpreted. It is a sign to unbelievers, is to be limited to two or three speakers in turn with an interpreter, and is not to be forbidden.

l: prophesying, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: Prophesying speaks to men for edification, exhortation, and consolation, and edifies the assembly, so the one who prophesies is greater than the one who speaks in languages without interpretation. It is a sign to believers, two or three prophets are to speak in turn while others discern, and all can prophesy one by one so that all may learn and be exhorted.

l: spiritual gifts, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: The believers are told to earnestly desire spiritual gifts, especially prophesying. Since they are zealous for them, they should use them to abound in building up the assembly.

l: wives, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: Wives are told to be quiet in the assemblies, as it has not been permitted for them to talk except in submission, as the law also says. If they desire to learn anything, they are to ask their own husbands at home, since it is shameful for a wife to talk in the assembly.

l: order and peace in worship, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 14
s: Because God is not a God of confusion but of peace, the chapter regulates who speaks and when: tongue speakers in turn with an interpreter or silence, prophets one by one with others discerning, and the first speaker yielding when a revelation comes to another. The chapter ends with the instruction that all things be done decently and in order.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: The speaker, who is named in the text only as the one who preached to the brothers, restates the Good News he delivered: Christ died for sins, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the twelve, over five hundred brothers, James, all the apostles, and finally to the speaker himself, who calls himself the least of the apostles because he persecuted the assembly of God. He argues against those among the addressed brothers who deny the resurrection of the dead, saying that if there is no resurrection then Christ was not raised, preaching and faith are vain, and believers remain in their sins. He affirms that Christ has been raised as the first fruits, that as in Adam all die so in Christ all will be made alive, and that Christ will reign until death, the last enemy, is abolished and the Son is subjected to God so that God may be all in all. He answers how the dead are raised using the images of seed and differing bodies and glories, contrasting the perishable natural body with the imperishable spiritual body and the first man Adam with the last Adam. He declares a mystery that all will be changed at the last trumpet, death will be swallowed up in victory, and he urges the brothers to be steadfast because their labor in the Lord is not in vain.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: Christ died for sins according to the Scriptures, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the twelve, over five hundred brothers, James, all the apostles, and the speaker. He is the first fruits of those asleep, will reign until all enemies are under his feet, and will then deliver up the Kingdom to God the Father and himself be subjected to God. He is called the last Adam, a life-giving spirit, and the second man, the Lord from heaven.

l: God, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: God raised Christ, gave the speaker grace that was not futile, and gives each seed a body as it pleased him. He subjected all things to Christ, excepting himself, and Christ will deliver the Kingdom to him so that God may be all in all. He gives believers the victory through the Lord Jesus Christ.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: The speaker, who preached the Good News to the brothers, delivered what he had also received and names himself as the last to whom Christ appeared, the least of the apostles, unworthy of the name because he persecuted the assembly of God. He says that by God's grace he worked more than all of them, that he dies daily, and that he fought with animals at Ephesus. He tells the mystery of the change at the last trumpet and exhorts the brothers to be steadfast.

l: Adam, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: The first man Adam is the one through whom death came and in whom all die. He became a living soul, was of the earth and made of dust, and is contrasted with Christ as the last Adam, a life-giving spirit. Humans have borne the image of those made of dust, as of him.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: The addressed brothers received the Good News, stand in it, and are saved if they hold firmly to it. Some among them say there is no resurrection of the dead, and the speaker rebukes this, warns them not to be deceived, and says some have no knowledge of God, to their shame. He closes by calling them beloved brothers to be steadfast, immovable, and abounding in the Lord's work.

l: resurrection of the dead, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: Its reality is tied to Christ's: if the dead are not raised, Christ was not raised, preaching and faith are vain, and those asleep in Christ have perished. It came by man, as death did, and Christ's resurrection as first fruits is followed by those who are Christ's at his coming. The speaker defends it against objections about how and with what body, and mentions people being baptized for the dead as a point in its favor.

l: Good News, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: The Good News is what the speaker preached and the brothers received, by which they are saved if they hold firmly to it. Its core, delivered first of all, is that Christ died for our sins, was buried, and was raised on the third day according to the Scriptures, as confirmed by many appearances. The speaker says that whether it is he or the others, so they preach and so the brothers believed.

l: death, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: Death came by man and in Adam all die. It is the last enemy to be abolished, and at the change of the perishable into the imperishable it will be swallowed up in victory. Its sting is sin, and the power of sin is the law.

l: resurrection body, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 15
s: The body is sown perishable, in dishonor, and in weakness as a natural body, and is raised imperishable, in glory, and in power as a spiritual body. The speaker compares it to a seed that dies and receives a body from God, and to the differing glories of celestial and terrestrial bodies. Flesh and blood cannot inherit God's Kingdom, so the perishable must put on imperishability and the mortal immortality.

l: Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: Paul closes his letter by instructing the Corinthians, as he did the assemblies of Galatia, to set aside money weekly for the collection for the saints, to be carried to Jerusalem by men they approve. He outlines his travel plans: he will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost because of a great open door and many adversaries, then pass through Macedonia and hopefully stay or winter with the Corinthians. He asks them to receive Timothy without fear and send him on in peace, reports that Apollos will come when he has opportunity, and urges them to honor the house of Stephanas and to acknowledge Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus. He ends with greetings from the assemblies of Asia, Aquila and Priscilla, and all the brothers, a curse on anyone who doesn't love the Lord Jesus Christ, and a blessing of grace and love.

l: Paul, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: Paul gives instructions for the collection and explains his travel plans: he will stay at Ephesus until Pentecost, then pass through Macedonia and hopes to stay or winter with the Corinthians. He urges Apollos to visit, commends Timothy and the house of Stephanas, and authenticates the closing greeting with his own hand. He ends with a curse on those who don't love the Lord and an expression of love to all of them in Christ Jesus.

l: collection for the saints, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: Paul directs the Corinthians, as he did the assemblies of Galatia, to save on the first day of every week as each may prosper so no collections are needed when he comes. Men approved by the Corinthians will carry the gift with letters to Jerusalem, and they will go with Paul if it is appropriate for him to go.

l: Timothy, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: Timothy may come to the Corinthians, and Paul asks that he be with them without fear because he does the Lord's work as Paul does. They are to let no one despise him and to send him on his way in peace so he can come to Paul, who expects him with the brothers.

l: Apollos, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: Paul says he strongly urged Apollos, called the brother, to come to the Corinthians with the brothers. It was not at all Apollos's desire to come now, but he will come when he has an opportunity.

l: household of Stephanas, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: Stephanas's house is identified as the first fruits of Achaia, and its members have set themselves to serve the saints. Paul asks the Corinthians to be in subjection to such people, and rejoices at the coming of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus, who supplied what was lacking on the Corinthians' part and refreshed Paul's spirit and theirs.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: Referred to as the Lord Jesus Christ, he is the one whom anyone who does not love is to be cursed. The text includes the prayer 'Come, Lord!' and asks that his grace be with the Corinthians, with Paul's love extended to them in Christ Jesus.

l: Corinthian believers (the readers), Paul’s First Letter to the Corinthians, Chapter 16
s: The Corinthians are told to save weekly for the collection, approve men to carry it to Jerusalem, receive Timothy without fear, and send him on in peace. They are urged to be in subjection to the house of Stephanas and others who labor, to acknowledge such people, and to stand firm, be courageous, and do everything in love. They receive greetings from the assemblies of Asia, Aquila and Priscilla with the assembly in their house, and all the brothers, and are told to greet one another with a holy kiss.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: In 2 Corinthians 1, Paul and Timothy greet the assembly of God at Corinth and all the saints in Achaia, blessing God as the Father of mercies and God of all comfort. Paul explains that God comforts him in affliction so he can comfort others, and he describes an affliction in Asia in which he and his companions despaired of life, learning to trust in God who raises the dead. He asks for the Corinthians' prayers and defends his conduct as holy and sincere. He then explains his changed travel plans, insisting he was not fickle, because God's promises are "Yes" in Jesus Christ. He says he did not come to Corinth in order to spare them, and that he and his companions are fellow workers for their joy rather than controllers of their faith.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by God's will, writes with Timothy to the Corinthians and describes being comforted by God in affliction so he can comfort others. He recounts despairing of life in Asia, defends his sincerity and his changed travel plans, and says he did not come to Corinth in order to spare them.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: The assembly at Corinth, along with all the saints in Achaia, is addressed by Paul and Timothy. They are told that Paul's afflictions and comforts serve their comfort and salvation, that they share in the sufferings and the comfort, and that their prayers help Paul. They are said to stand firm in faith, and Paul claims they are his boasting as he is theirs.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: God is called the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts in all affliction and raises the dead. He delivered Paul from great death, is hoped in for further deliverance, and is called faithful. He establishes and anoints Paul and his companions, and has sealed them and given the Spirit as a down payment in their hearts.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is the Lord and the Son of God, preached among the Corinthians by Paul, Silvanus, and Timothy. The sufferings of Christ abound to Paul's group, and comfort abounds through Christ. In him all God's promises are "Yes," and through him comes the "Amen" to God's glory.

l: comfort, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Comfort comes from God, who comforts Paul in all affliction so that he can comfort others with the same comfort. It abounds through Christ and produces in the Corinthians patient endurance of the same sufferings. Paul's hope for them is steadfast because they share in the comfort as they share in the sufferings.

l: affliction and sufferings, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Paul says the sufferings of Christ abound to him and that his afflictions serve the Corinthians' comfort and salvation. The Corinthians are partakers of the same sufferings and endure them patiently. These afflictions come with God's comfort.

l: Paul's affliction in Asia, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Paul says that in Asia he and his companions were weighed down exceedingly, beyond their power, to the point of despairing of life. They felt they had received the sentence of death, which taught them to trust in God who raises the dead rather than in themselves. God delivered them from so great a death, and Paul hopes he will deliver them again.

l: Paul's travel plans, 2 Corinthians, Paul’s Second Letter to the Corinthians / Chapter 1
s: Paul had planned to come to the Corinthians first, pass on to Macedonia, return to them from Macedonia, and be sent on by them to Judea. He denies that changing these plans showed fickleness or fleshly planning, and says his word to them was not "Yes and no." He states he did not come to Corinth in order to spare them.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: In this chapter the author, writing in the first person, explains that he decided not to come to the recipients again in sorrow, and that he wrote to them out of much affliction and many tears to show his abundant love, not to grieve them. He says that the one who caused sorrow has grieved all of them in part, that the punishment inflicted by the many is sufficient, and that they should now forgive and comfort that person and confirm their love for him lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. He says he forgives whomever they forgive, in the presence of Christ, so that Satan gains no advantage, since they are not ignorant of his schemes. He recounts that at Troas, despite an open door in the Lord, he had no relief because he did not find Titus his brother, and so he went on into Macedonia. He closes by thanking God who leads them in triumph in Christ and spreads the sweet aroma of his knowledge, being a stench of death to those who perish and a sweet aroma of life to those being saved, and he says they speak sincerely in Christ and do not peddle the word of God.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: Paul says he decided not to come again in sorrow, and that he wrote out of much affliction, anguish and many tears to make known his abundant love. He urges the recipients to forgive and comfort the offender, says he forgives whomever they forgive for their sakes in Christ's presence, and recounts having no relief at Troas for not finding Titus, so he went to Macedonia. He declares that he and his companions speak sincerely in Christ and do not peddle God's word.

l: Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: The recipients are told they were caused sorrow in part by the offender, and that the punishment inflicted by the many on him is sufficient. They are urged to forgive and comfort him and to confirm their love toward him, and their obedience in all things was the proof Paul sought by writing.

l: offender (the one who caused sorrow), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: He is described as having caused sorrow not chiefly to Paul but in part to all of the recipients. He has received a punishment inflicted by the many, which is declared sufficient, and Paul asks that he be forgiven and comforted lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: Christ is the one in whose presence Paul forgives for the recipients' sakes, and the Good News of Christ is what brought Paul to Troas. God leads Paul and his companions in triumph in Christ, they are a sweet aroma of Christ to God, and they speak in Christ.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: Paul gives thanks to God, who always leads them in triumph in Christ and reveals through them the sweet aroma of his knowledge in every place. Paul says they speak in God's sight, from God, and not as peddlers of God's word.

l: sorrow (grief caused by Paul's earlier letter), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: Paul says he would not come again in sorrow, and that his letter was written not to make the recipients grieve but so they would know his love. He notes that whoever caused sorrow did so in part to them all, and that the offender risks being swallowed up by excessive sorrow.

l: forgiveness, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 2
s: Paul urges the recipients to forgive the offender, comfort him, and confirm their love toward him. He states that he forgives whomever they forgive, doing so for their sakes in Christ's presence, so that Satan gains no advantage over them.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: In this chapter the writer, speaking for himself and his co-workers, asks whether they need letters of commendation and answers that the Corinthian believers themselves are Christ's letter, written by the Spirit of the living God on hearts of flesh. He says their sufficiency comes from God, who made them servants of a new covenant of the Spirit rather than of the letter. He contrasts the service written on stones, which came with a glory so bright that the children of Israel could not look at Moses' face, with the Spirit's service, which has much more glory and remains. Moses put a veil on his face, and the same veil still lies on the hearts of those who read the old covenant, until someone turns to the Lord. Where the Spirit of the Lord is there is liberty, and believers with unveiled faces are transformed into the Lord's image from glory to glory.

l: Moses, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Moses' face was so glorious that the children of Israel could not look steadily at it, and the glory was passing away. He put a veil on his face so that they would not look at the end of that fading glory. To this day, when Moses is read, a veil lies on the heart of those who hear.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Christ is the one whose letter the Corinthian believers are shown to be, a letter served by Paul and his co-workers. Through Christ they have confidence toward God. In Christ the veil over the reading of the old covenant passes away.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: God is the source of the writers' sufficiency and the one who made them sufficient as servants of a new covenant. He is called the living God, whose Spirit writes on hearts. The confidence of the writers toward him comes through Christ.

l: Holy Spirit, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The Spirit of the living God writes the Corinthians as a letter on hearts of flesh, and he gives life, in contrast to the letter, which kills. The Lord is identified as the Spirit, and where the Spirit of the Lord is there is liberty. The Spirit is also the one from whom believers are transformed from glory to glory, and his service has much more glory.

l: children of Israel, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The children of Israel could not look steadily at Moses' face because of its glory. Moses veiled his face so they would not see the end of the passing glory. Their minds were hardened, and a veil remains over their hearts when Moses is read.

l: Paul and his fellow ministers (we), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The writers ask whether they are commending themselves again and say they need no letters of commendation. They say they are not sufficient of themselves, but God made them sufficient as servants of a new covenant. Because of their hope they speak with great boldness, unlike Moses, and they, with all believers, are transformed with unveiled faces.

l: Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The Corinthian believers are described as the writers' letter, written in their hearts, known and read by all, and revealed as a letter of Christ. It was written with the Spirit of the living God on hearts of flesh, not with ink on stone tablets. They serve as the writers' commendation.

l: new covenant, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The new covenant is one of the Spirit, not of the letter, and God made the writers sufficient as its servants. Its service is a service of righteousness and exceeds in glory the earlier service. It remains, and it gives life.

l: old covenant, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The old covenant is described as a service of death and condemnation, engraved on stones, which came with glory that was passing away. The same veil remains at its reading to this day, because the veil passes away only in Christ. The letter, in contrast to the Spirit, kills.

l: veil, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: The veil was put on Moses' face so the children of Israel would not look at the end of the fading glory. It remains at the reading of the old covenant and lies on the heart when Moses is read. It is taken away whenever someone turns to the Lord, and believers have unveiled faces.

l: glory, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 3
s: Glory marked the service of death and condemnation, seen in Moses' face, but that glory was passing away. The service of the Spirit and of righteousness has much more glory and remains. Believers who see the Lord's glory as in a mirror are transformed into his image from glory to glory.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: In this chapter the ministers explain that, having received mercy through their ministry, they do not lose heart, and they have renounced shameful, deceitful ways in favor of openly stating the truth. They say the Good News is veiled only to those who are dying, whose minds the god of this world has blinded so they cannot see the light of the glory of Christ. They preach Christ Jesus as Lord and themselves as servants of the believers, and they describe carrying the treasure of God's light in clay vessels, so that the greatness of the power is from God. Though pressed, perplexed, pursued and struck down, they are not crushed, forsaken or destroyed, and they always carry the dying of Jesus so that his life may be revealed in them. They hold to the hope that God, who raised the Lord Jesus, will raise them and present them with the believers, and they look at unseen eternal things rather than seen temporal ones.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: God is the one who said light would shine out of darkness and has shone in the ministers' hearts to give the light of the knowledge of his glory in the face of Jesus Christ. He is the source of the exceeding greatness of power, and he raised the Lord Jesus and will raise the ministers also and present them with the believers. The multiplied grace is meant to cause thanksgiving to abound to his glory.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: Jesus Christ is described as the image of God, whose glory is the subject of the Good News, and he is preached as Lord. His putting to death is carried in the ministers' bodies so that his life may be revealed in their mortal flesh. God raised him, and through him God will raise the ministers.

l: Paul and his fellow ministers (we), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The ministers say they do not faint because they have received mercy and have this ministry. They have renounced shameful hidden things and deceit, preach Christ Jesus as Lord rather than themselves, and see themselves as servants of the believers for Jesus' sake. Though their outward person decays, their inward person is renewed daily, and they fix their gaze on unseen, eternal things.

l: Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The believers are those for whose sake the ministers serve and for whose sake all things happen. Life works in them while death works in the ministers. The ministers expect God to present them together with the believers, and the grace multiplied through many leads to abounding thanksgiving.

l: Good News of Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The Good News is the message of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God. It is veiled to those who are dying, whose minds the god of this world has blinded so that its light does not dawn on them. The ministers commend themselves by the truth and do not handle the word of God deceitfully.

l: treasure in clay vessels, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The ministers say they have this treasure in clay vessels, meaning the light of the knowledge of God's glory in their hearts held in frail bodies. This is so that the exceeding greatness of the power may be seen to be of God and not from themselves.

l: affliction and suffering, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 4
s: The ministers are pressed on every side, perplexed, pursued and struck down, yet not crushed, driven to despair, forsaken or destroyed. They are always delivered to death for Jesus' sake so that his life is revealed in them. Their light affliction, lasting only a moment, works for them an eternal weight of glory far beyond it.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: The speaker, writing for himself and his fellow ministers, contrasts the earthly tent of the body with a house from God, eternal in the heavens, and says they groan to be clothed with it so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. God has given the Spirit as a down payment, so they are confident, walk by faith, and aim to please the Lord whether at home in the body or absent from it. All must be revealed before the judgment seat of Christ to receive according to what they have done in the body. The love of Christ compels them because one died for all, so that the living should live for him who died and rose. Anyone in Christ is a new creation, and God, who reconciled us through Christ, has given the ministry of reconciliation, so the ministers act as ambassadors urging people to be reconciled to God, since he made the sinless one to be sin so that we might become the righteousness of God.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: God made us for the purpose of being clothed with our heavenly habitation and gave the Spirit as a down payment. He reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ, was in Christ reconciling the world and not reckoning trespasses to them, and entrusted the word of reconciliation to the ministers. He made the sinless one to be sin on our behalf so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Christ's love compels the ministers, who judge that he died for all, so that those who live should live for him who died and rose again. God was in Christ reconciling the world to himself. He knew no sin but was made to be sin on our behalf, and he holds the judgment seat before which all must be revealed.

l: Paul and his fellow ministers (we), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: The ministers groan in the tent, long to be clothed with the heavenly habitation, and are confident, walking by faith and not by sight. They aim to please the Lord, persuade men knowing the fear of the Lord, and are compelled by Christ's love. They have been given the ministry and word of reconciliation and act as ambassadors for Christ, begging people to be reconciled to God.

l: earthly tent (our body), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: The earthly house of our tent may be dissolved, and in it we groan, being burdened. The desire is not to be unclothed but to be clothed, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life. While at home in the body we are absent from the Lord.

l: heavenly building (from God), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: It is a building from God, a house not made with hands, eternal, in the heavens. We groan longing to be clothed with this habitation from heaven, and we have it if the earthly tent is dissolved.

l: judgment seat of Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Before it we must all be revealed. Each one will receive the things done in the body, whether good or bad. Knowing this, the ministers persuade men in the fear of the Lord.

l: new creation, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Anyone who is in Christ is a new creation. The old things have passed away and all things have become new. This is tied to no longer knowing anyone according to the flesh.

l: reconciliation, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 5
s: Reconciliation is from God, who reconciled us to himself through Jesus Christ and gave the ministry and word of reconciliation to the ministers. God was in Christ reconciling the world, not reckoning trespasses to them. The ministers, as ambassadors, plead with people to be reconciled to God.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The speaker, writing on behalf of himself and his co-workers, urges the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain, citing a saying of God that now is the acceptable time and the day of salvation. He and his co-workers describe how they commend themselves as servants of God by giving no cause for stumbling, enduring afflictions, beatings, imprisonments, and fastings, and by living in pureness, knowledge, kindness, the Holy Spirit, and sincere love. They present paradoxes of their ministry: dying yet living, sorrowful yet rejoicing, poor yet making many rich. The speaker says his heart is open to the Corinthians, who are restricted by their own affections rather than by him, and asks them to open their hearts in return. He then tells them not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, contrasting righteousness with iniquity, light with darkness, Christ with Belial, and the temple of God with idols, and closes with God's promise to be a Father to those who come out and are separate.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: God is quoted as saying he listened to and helped his people at an acceptable time, in a day of salvation. His servants commend themselves by the power of God. He declares that he will dwell in and walk among his people, be their God, receive them, and be a Father to them as sons and daughters, and he is called the Lord Almighty.

l: Paul and his fellow ministers (we), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The speaker and his co-workers entreat the Corinthians not to receive God's grace in vain and give no occasion of stumbling so their service is not blamed. They commend themselves as servants of God through endurance, sufferings, and virtues, and are described by paradoxes such as dying yet living and having nothing yet possessing all things. They say their mouth and heart are open to the Corinthians and ask for the same in return, speaking to them as to children.

l: Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The Corinthians are urged not to receive God's grace in vain and are told that they are restricted not by the apostles but by their own affections. They are asked to open their hearts in return, are warned not to be unequally yoked with unbelievers, and are identified as a temple of the living God. They are called to come out from among unbelievers and be separate, with the promise that God will receive them.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: Christ appears in a rhetorical question: what agreement does Christ have with Belial? This is used to show that believers should not be yoked with unbelievers.

l: day of salvation, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The day of salvation is drawn from a quoted saying about an acceptable time when God listened and helped. The text declares that now is the acceptable time and now is the day of salvation, which gives urgency to the plea not to receive God's grace in vain.

l: hardships and sufferings of the apostles' ministry, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The ministry's sufferings are listed as great endurance, afflictions, hardships, distresses, beatings, imprisonments, riots, labors, watchings, and fastings. They are part of how the apostles commend themselves as servants of God, alongside glory and dishonor, evil and good report, and being punished yet not killed. They are paired with paradoxes of sorrow yet rejoicing and poverty yet making many rich.

l: unbelievers, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: Unbelievers are those with whom the Corinthians are told not to be unequally yoked. The text asks what fellowship, agreement, or portion righteousness, light, Christ, and a believer can have with iniquity, darkness, Belial, and an unbeliever. The call to come out from among them and touch no unclean thing follows.

l: temple of the living God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 6
s: The Corinthians are identified as a temple of the living God, which has no agreement with idols. God is quoted as promising to dwell in them and walk in them, being their God while they are his people.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: The speaker urges the beloved recipients to cleanse themselves and open their hearts, asserting that he and his companions wronged, corrupted, and took advantage of no one. He describes affliction in Macedonia, with fightings outside and fear inside, until God comforted them through the coming of Titus, who brought news of the recipients' longing, mourning, and zeal. The speaker explains that his earlier letter grieved them only for a while, and that he rejoices because their grief led to repentance, distinguishing godly sorrow that leads to salvation from worldly sorrow that produces death. He says he wrote so that their earnest care for him would be revealed before God, and that Titus was refreshed by them all. The speaker's boasts about them to Titus proved true, and he closes by rejoicing in his confidence concerning them.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Paul urges the recipients to cleanse themselves and open their hearts, insisting that he and his companions wronged, corrupted, and took advantage of no one. He recounts affliction in Macedonia and being comforted by Titus's coming. He admits he regretted sending his letter but no longer does, rejoices over their repentance, and ends confident in them.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: The recipients are called beloved and urged to cleanse themselves and open their hearts to the author. They were grieved by his letter to repentance, showing earnest care, defense, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and vindication, and proving themselves pure in the matter. They refreshed Titus's spirit and received him with fear and trembling, and the author is confident concerning them in everything.

l: Titus, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Titus's coming comforted the author and his companions in Macedonia, and he reported the recipients' longing, mourning, and zeal. His spirit was refreshed by all of them, and the author rejoiced the more for his joy. The author's boasts about the recipients to Titus proved true, and Titus's affection toward them is abundant as he remembers their obedience.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: God is described as the one who comforts the lowly, and he comforted the author and his companions through the coming of Titus. The recipients' earnest care for the author was to be revealed in the sight of God. The text also frames holiness as perfected in the fear of God, and grief that is godly as being according to him.

l: letter (Paul's letter to the Corinthians), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: The letter grieved the recipients, though only for a while, and the author regretted sending it before ceasing to regret it. It led them to repentance. He says he wrote it neither for the sake of the one who did wrong nor the one who suffered wrong, but so that the recipients' earnest care for him would be revealed before God.

l: godly sorrow, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Godly sorrow is said to produce repentance leading to salvation, which brings no regret, in contrast to the sorrow of the world, which produces death. The recipients were grieved in a godly way and so suffered no loss through the author. It worked in them earnest care, defense, indignation, fear, longing, zeal, and vindication.

l: comfort, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 7
s: Comfort is a central theme: the author overflows with comfort and joy despite affliction, and God comforted him and his companions through Titus's coming. This comfort also came from the comfort Titus received in the recipients. The author and his companions rejoiced all the more because Titus's spirit was refreshed by them.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: The writer, speaking to the brothers, holds up the assemblies of Macedonia as an example: despite severe affliction and deep poverty they gave generously, beyond their power and of their own accord, first giving themselves to the Lord. Because of this, the writer urged Titus to complete among the addressees the grace of giving he had begun. The addressees, who abound in faith, utterance, knowledge and love, are urged to abound in this grace too, following the example of Jesus Christ, who became poor so they might become rich. Giving should match what one has, aiming at equality so that present abundance and later abundance supply each other's lack. Titus and two other brothers are sent to administer the gift honorably, and the addressees are asked to show proof of their love to them.

l: assemblies of Macedonia, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: The assemblies of Macedonia, in a severe ordeal of affliction and deep poverty, gave with abundant joy, according to and beyond their power, of their own accord. They begged for the fellowship in the service to the saints, and first gave themselves to the Lord and to the writer's party through the will of God.

l: Titus, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Titus was urged to complete among the addressees the grace he had previously begun. He accepted the exhortation, and being very earnest he went out to them of his own accord. The writer calls him his partner and fellow worker for the addressees.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Jesus Christ is cited as the model of grace: though he was rich, for the addressees' sakes he became poor, so that through his poverty they might become rich.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: God is credited with the grace given in the Macedonian assemblies and with putting the same earnest care for the addressees into Titus's heart. Thanks are given to him, and the Macedonians' giving came through his will.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: The addressees are said to abound in faith, utterance, knowledge, earnestness and love, and are urged to abound in this grace as well. They were first to start a year ago, and are told to complete the doing as they had been ready to be willing, according to what they have. They are asked to show proof of their love to the sent brothers before the assemblies.

l: grace of giving (collection for the saints), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: The grace of giving is a service to the saints that the Macedonians pleaded to share in, and that Titus is to complete among the addressees. It is acceptable according to what one has, and is administered by the writer's party to the Lord's glory and to show readiness, with care to be honorable before the Lord and before men.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: The writer makes known the Macedonians' grace, urges Titus to complete the work, and gives advice rather than commandment to test the sincerity of the addressees' love. He sends Titus with two brothers, and takes care to avoid any blame concerning the abundance he administers. He also speaks of his boasting on the addressees' behalf.

l: equality, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 8
s: Equality is the stated purpose of the giving: not that others be eased and the addressees distressed. Their present abundance supplies others' lack so that others' abundance may later supply theirs, as with the gathered manna where he who gathered much had nothing left over and he who gathered little had no lack.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: In Chapter 9 the writer, Paul, tells the believers in Achaia that he need not write at length about the service to the saints, since he knows their readiness and has boasted of it to those in Macedonia. He sends the brothers ahead so that the promised gift will be ready and so that his boasting is not shown to be empty if Macedonians come with him and find Achaia unprepared. He teaches that sowing sparingly brings a sparing harvest, sowing bountifully a bountiful one, and that each should give willingly because God loves a cheerful giver. He explains that God supplies and multiplies seed and the fruits of righteousness. The service of giving meets the saints' needs and produces thanksgiving to God, and the saints will glorify God and yearn for the givers; the chapter closes with thanks to God for his unspeakable gift.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Paul writes that it is unnecessary to write about the service to the saints, since he has boasted of Achaia's readiness to the Macedonians. He sends the brothers ahead so his boasting will not prove empty, and he teaches that giving should be bountiful and cheerful rather than grudging. He closes by giving thanks to God for his unspeakable gift.

l: Achaia, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Achaia is said to have been prepared for the past year, and its zeal stirred up very many of the Macedonians. Paul fears it may be found unprepared if Macedonians come with him, so he sends the brothers to make sure its promised gift is ready.

l: Macedonia, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Paul has boasted to those of Macedonia about Achaia's readiness, and Achaia's zeal stirred up very many of them. Paul notes that some from Macedonia may come with him and find Achaia unprepared.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: God loves a cheerful giver and is able to make all grace abound so that the givers have all sufficiency and abound in every good work. He supplies seed to the sower and bread for food, multiplies the seed, and increases the fruits of righteousness. Thanksgiving and glory are given to him through the giving, and Paul thanks him for his unspeakable gift.

l: saints, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: The saints are the recipients of the service of giving, which makes up for their lack. They will glorify God for the givers' obedience and generosity, and with supplication they yearn for the givers because of the exceeding grace of God in them.

l: brothers (from Macedonia), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: Paul has sent the brothers, entreating them to go ahead to Achaia and arrange the promised generous gift beforehand. Their purpose is that Paul's boasting not be in vain and that the gift be ready as generosity, not greediness.

l: grace of giving (collection for the saints), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 9
s: The gift was promised by the Achaians earlier and is to be arranged ahead of time so that it is ready as a matter of generosity, not greediness. Each person is to give as determined in the heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion. It makes up for lack among the saints and produces much thanksgiving to God.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: In this chapter Paul appeals to the Corinthian audience by the humility and gentleness of Christ, saying he is lowly in person but bold when absent, and he hopes not to have to be bold against critics who think he walks according to the flesh. He explains that his weapons of warfare are mighty before God for throwing down strongholds, imaginations and every high thing raised against the knowledge of God, and for bringing every thought captive to Christ. He defends his authority, given by the Lord for building up, against the charge that his letters are strong but his presence and speech are weak, insisting that he is the same in deed as in word. He contrasts himself with self-commending rivals who measure themselves by themselves, saying he boasts only within the limits God appointed, which reach to Corinth. He hopes to preach beyond them as their faith grows, and concludes that one should boast in the Lord, since the one the Lord commends is approved.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Paul entreats the Corinthians by the humility and gentleness of Christ and admits he is said to be lowly in person but bold when absent. He claims he walks in the flesh but does not wage war according to it, defends his authority, and insists he is the same in deed as in his letters. He says he boasts only within the limits God appointed, reaching to Corinth, and hopes to preach the Good News in regions beyond them.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Christ's humility and gentleness are the basis of Paul's entreaty, and every thought is to be brought into captivity to the obedience of Christ. Paul says that anyone who trusts he belongs to Christ should consider that Paul also belongs to Christ. The Good News of Christ is what Paul brought as far as Corinth.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: The Corinthians are urged by Paul to look beyond how things appear and are told he hopes not to need to show boldness when he is present. Their obedience is to be made full, and Paul hopes that as their faith grows he will be enlarged among them in his sphere so as to preach beyond them. They are within the boundaries God appointed to Paul.

l: critics (those who consider Paul to walk according to the flesh), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: These critics consider Paul and his companions to be walking according to the flesh, and they say his letters are weighty and strong but his bodily presence is weak and his speech despised. Paul tells such a person to consider that he is in deed when present what he is in word by letters when absent. He also tells them he is ready to avenge disobedience once the Corinthians' obedience is full.

l: self-commending rivals (those who commend themselves), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: These people commend themselves, measuring themselves by themselves and comparing themselves with themselves, and Paul says they are without understanding. Paul declines to number or compare himself with them. Their way of boasting is contrasted with approval that comes from the Lord's commendation.

l: spiritual warfare (weapons against strongholds), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Paul says that though he walks in the flesh, he does not wage war according to the flesh. The weapons of this warfare are mighty before God for throwing down strongholds, imaginations and every high thing exalted against the knowledge of God, and for bringing every thought captive to the obedience of Christ.

l: apostolic authority, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Paul's authority was given by the Lord for building the Corinthians up and not for casting them down, and he says he will not be ashamed of boasting somewhat abundantly about it. He denies wanting to terrify them by his letters, and says his authority is the same in presence as in writing. Its boundaries are appointed by God and reach to Corinth.

l: boasting, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 10
s: Paul says he will not boast beyond proper limits or in other men's labors, but only within the boundaries God appointed to him. He quotes that whoever boasts should boast in the Lord. He adds that approval comes not to the one who commends himself but to the one whom the Lord commends.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: In Chapter 11 Paul expresses godly jealousy for the Corinthians, whom he promised to one husband, Christ, and fears they will be led astray from simple devotion to Christ as the serpent deceived Eve. He defends his standing against the very best apostles, reminding them that he preached God's Good News free of charge, supported by brothers from Macedonia, and will keep doing so. He denounces false apostles as deceitful workers who masquerade as apostles of Christ, just as Satan masquerades as an angel of light. Reluctantly boasting as a fool, he lists his Hebrew heritage and his labors, prisons, beatings, stoning, shipwrecks, perils, hardships and daily anxiety for all the assemblies. He ends by choosing to boast of his weakness, recalling his escape from the governor under King Aretas in Damascus by being let down in a basket through a window in the wall.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Paul feels godly jealousy for the Corinthians and fears they will be corrupted from the simplicity in Christ. He defends himself as not behind the best apostles, claims to be a Hebrew, Israelite and offspring of Abraham, and recounts his hardships. He escaped arrest in Damascus by being let down in a basket through a window in the wall.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: The Corinthians are said to have been promised in marriage to one husband, Christ, to be presented as a pure virgin. Paul fears their minds will be deceived and rebukes them for putting up with anyone who preaches another Jesus, a different spirit or a different good news. He also says they bear with those who bring them into bondage, devour them, take them captive, exalt themselves or strike them on the face.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Christ is the one husband to whom Paul promised the Corinthians, so that he might present them as a pure virgin. Paul speaks of the simplicity that is in Christ and of the truth of Christ being in him, and he warns against false apostles who masquerade as Christ's apostles.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: God is the source of the Good News Paul preached free of charge, and he is called upon to know that Paul loves the Corinthians. He is also called the God and Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, blessed forever, who knows Paul does not lie.

l: false apostles, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Paul calls them false apostles and deceitful workers who masquerade as Christ's apostles, like Satan who masquerades as an angel of light. They are said to be servants of Satan who masquerade as servants of righteousness, and their end will be according to their works. Paul acts to cut off the opportunity of those who desire to be recognized as equal to him.

l: Paul's sufferings, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Paul lists his labors, prisons, stripes above measure and frequent deaths. These include five times receiving forty stripes minus one from the Jews, three beatings with rods, one stoning, three shipwrecks, and a night and a day in the deep. He adds many perils, hunger, thirst, cold, nakedness and daily anxiety for all the assemblies.

l: boasting, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Paul boasts reluctantly and as foolishness, saying it is not according to the Lord, because many boast after the flesh. He compares his credentials and sufferings with those of his rivals, and then resolves to boast of the things that concern his weakness. He closes with the Damascus escape in a basket as an example.

l: Paul's free preaching, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 11
s: Paul preached God's Good News to the Corinthians free of charge, humbling himself so that they might be exalted. He took wages from other assemblies to serve them, and brothers from Macedonia supplied his need so he was no burden to anyone. He vows to continue this in the regions of Achaia, to cut off opportunity from those who want to boast.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: In this chapter the speaker, who is Paul, reluctantly turns to visions and revelations of the Lord and describes a man in Christ who was caught up into the third heaven and Paradise fourteen years earlier and heard unspeakable words. Paul says he will boast only of such a man and of his own weaknesses, and that to keep him from being exalted excessively he was given a thorn in the flesh, a messenger of Satan. He begged the Lord three times for its removal, and the Lord answered that his grace is sufficient and his power is made perfect in weakness. Paul then defends his apostleship to the Corinthian believers, reminding them of the signs and wonders worked among them and that he was never a financial burden to them, and he says he is ready to come a third time. He closes by fearing that he will find strife, factions and other disorders among them, and that he will mourn for those who have sinned and not repented of uncleanness, sexual immorality and lustfulness.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
