s: Paul reluctantly turns to boasting, saying he will boast only on behalf of the man caught up to Paradise and in his own weaknesses. He reports that a thorn in the flesh was given him, that the Lord told him grace is sufficient, and that he takes pleasure in weaknesses for Christ's sake. He defends his apostleship, denies burdening or deceiving the Corinthians, and says he will gladly spend and be spent for their souls.

l: man in Christ (caught up into Paradise), 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Paul says he knows a man in Christ who fourteen years earlier was caught up into the third heaven, into Paradise, whether in or out of the body being known only to God. The man heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter, and Paul says he will boast on behalf of such a one.

l: Lord, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: The Lord is the source of the visions and revelations Paul mentions. When Paul begged him three times about the thorn, he replied that his grace is sufficient and that his power is made perfect in weakness.

l: thorn in the flesh, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: The thorn in the flesh, described as a messenger of Satan to torment Paul, was given to him because of the exceeding greatness of the revelations, so that he would not be exalted excessively. Paul begged the Lord three times for it to depart, but it was not removed; he was told grace is sufficient.

l: visions and revelations, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Paul says he comes to visions and revelations of the Lord, illustrated by the man caught up to the third heaven and Paradise. Their exceeding greatness is given as the reason a thorn in the flesh was given to keep Paul from being exalted excessively.

l: boasting, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Paul calls boasting not profitable and says he has become foolish in it because the Corinthians compelled him. He will boast on behalf of the man caught up to Paradise and in his weaknesses but not on his own behalf, refraining so that no one thinks more of him than what they see or hear from him.

l: weakness, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Paul says he will boast in his weaknesses and glory in them so that the power of Christ may rest on him. He takes pleasure in weaknesses, injuries, necessities, persecutions and distresses for Christ's sake, concluding that when he is weak, then he is strong.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: The Corinthians are said to have compelled Paul to boast, and he reminds them that the signs of an apostle were worked among them. He tells them he seeks them and not their possessions, that all things are for their edifying, and that he fears finding them in strife, jealousy, factions and other disorders.

l: burden (financial) to the Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Paul says the Corinthians were not made inferior to other assemblies except that he was not a burden to them, and he asks forgiveness for this wrong. He affirms he will not burden them, since parents should save up for children, and he denies taking advantage of them himself or through Titus and the brother he sent.

l: upcoming visit to Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Paul says this is the third time he is ready to come to the Corinthians and that he will not be a burden to them. He fears that when he comes he will find them not as he wishes, and that God may humble him before them as he mourns over those who have sinned.

l: sins of the Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 12
s: Paul fears he may find strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, factions, slander, whisperings, proud thoughts and riots among the Corinthians. He also expects to mourn for many who have sinned and not repented of uncleanness, sexual immorality and lustfulness.

l: 2 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: In the closing chapter of the letter, Paul tells the Corinthian believers that he is coming to them a third time and warns those who have sinned that he will not spare them when he arrives. He says they are seeking proof that Christ speaks in him, and notes that Christ was crucified in weakness yet lives by God's power, as Paul and his companions are weak in him yet will live by that power toward them. Paul urges the Corinthians to examine and test themselves to see whether they are in the faith and whether Jesus Christ is in them. He prays that they do what is honorable and become perfect, and explains that he writes while absent so that he need not deal sharply when present, using the authority the Lord gave him for building up. He ends with final exhortations to rejoice, be perfected, be of one mind and live in peace, greetings from all the saints, and a benediction naming the Lord Jesus Christ, God, and the Holy Spirit.

l: Paul, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: Paul announces he is coming a third time and warns that he will not spare those who have sinned, while writing in absence so he need not deal sharply in person. He says Christ speaks in him, that he and his companions are weak in Christ yet will live by God's power, and that he prays for the Corinthians to do good and become perfect. He closes with exhortations, greetings, and a benediction, noting his authority from the Lord is for building up and not tearing down.

l: Christ, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: Jesus Christ is said to speak in Paul and to be powerful in the Corinthians. He was crucified through weakness yet lives through the power of God. Paul says Christ is in the believers unless they are disqualified, and the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ is invoked on them in the closing benediction.

l: God, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: God's power is the source by which Christ lives and by which Paul and his companions will live with him toward the Corinthians. Paul prays to God that they do no evil, and calls him the God of love and peace who will be with them if they live in peace. God's love is named in the closing benediction.

l: assembly of God at Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: The Corinthians are warned, especially those who have sinned, that Paul will not spare them when he comes. They are seeking proof that Christ speaks in Paul, and are told to test themselves to see whether they are in the faith. They are exhorted to rejoice, be perfected, be comforted, be of the same mind, live in peace, and greet one another with a holy kiss, and they receive greetings from all the saints.

l: upcoming visit to Corinth, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: Paul says this will be his third coming to the Corinthians, after warning them during his second visit and now again in writing while absent. If he comes again he will not spare those who have sinned. He writes beforehand so he need not deal sharply when present, since his authority is for building up and not tearing down.

l: self-examination of faith, 2 Corinthians, Chapter 13
s: Paul commands the Corinthians to examine and test themselves to see whether they are in the faith, asking whether they do not know that Jesus Christ is in them, unless they are disqualified. He answers their demand for proof of Christ speaking in him by turning the test back on them, and he hopes they will know that he and his companions are not disqualified.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: Paul, an apostle commissioned through Jesus Christ and God the Father rather than by men, writes with the brothers who are with him to the assemblies of Galatia. After a greeting of grace and peace, he expresses astonishment that the Galatians are quickly deserting the one who called them for a different "good news," which he says is not another gospel but a perversion by those who trouble them. He pronounces a curse on anyone, even himself or an angel from heaven, who preaches a different gospel. He insists that the Good News he preached came not from man but through a revelation of Jesus Christ, and he recounts his former persecution of the assembly, his call by God, his time in Arabia and Damascus, his brief visit to Peter and James in Jerusalem, and his time in Syria and Cilicia, where the assemblies of Judea heard of his change and glorified God in him.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: Paul identifies himself as an apostle sent not from or through men but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, and he writes to the assemblies of Galatia with the brothers who are with him. He rebukes the Galatians for deserting the gospel, denies that he seeks to please men, and recounts his past: he persecuted and ravaged the assembly of God, excelled in the Jews' religion, was separated from his mother's womb and called by God's grace, went to Arabia and Damascus, then after three years visited Peter for fifteen days and saw James, and afterward went to Syria and Cilicia. He swears before God that he is not lying, and the assemblies of Judea, who knew him only by report, glorified God in him.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: Jesus Christ is named as the one through whom Paul is made an apostle, and he was raised from the dead by God the Father. He is called Lord, gave himself for sins to deliver people out of this present evil age according to God's will, and a revelation of him is how Paul received the Good News.

l: God the Father, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: God the Father, together with Jesus Christ, commissioned Paul as an apostle and raised Jesus from the dead; grace and peace come from him. He is the one to whom glory is due forever, and it was his good pleasure to separate Paul from his mother's womb, call him through grace, and reveal his Son in him so Paul might preach among the Gentiles.

l: Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: The Galatians, addressed as the assemblies of Galatia, are greeted with grace and peace and then rebuked because Paul marvels that they are so quickly deserting the one who called them in Christ's grace for a different "good news." They are being troubled by some who want to pervert the gospel, and Paul reminds them that they have heard of his former way of life in the Jews' religion.

l: Good News of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: The Good News of Christ is the gospel Paul preached and the Galatians received, and he says there is no other. He declares that it is not according to man, that he neither received it from man nor was taught it, and that anyone preaching something different is to be cursed.

l: different good news (false gospel), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: The different "good news" is the message to which the Galatians are turning, though Paul says it is not truly another good news. Paul says that anyone who preaches any "good news" other than what was preached and received, whether he, an angel from heaven, or any man, is to be cursed.

l: troublers (those perverting the gospel), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: The troublers are some people who trouble the Galatians and want to pervert the Good News of Christ. The text does not name them, but Paul says that anyone who preaches a different "good news" than the one received is to be cursed.

l: Paul's revelation, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians / Chapter 1
s: Paul states that the Good News he preaches came to him through a revelation of Jesus Christ, not from man and not by being taught. God was pleased to reveal his Son in Paul so that he might preach him among the Gentiles, and Paul did not immediately confer with flesh and blood or go up to Jerusalem, but went into Arabia and returned to Damascus.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: The speaker, Paul, recounts going up to Jerusalem after fourteen years with Barnabas and Titus, laying before the respected leaders the Good News he preaches to the Gentiles. Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised, and Paul refused to yield to the false brothers who sought to bring them into bondage. James, Cephas, and John gave Paul and Barnabas the right hand of fellowship, agreeing that they would go to the Gentiles and the leaders to the circumcision, asking only that they remember the poor. Paul then describes resisting Peter to his face at Antioch, where Peter withdrew from eating with Gentiles for fear of those from James, and the other Jews and Barnabas followed him. Paul argues that a person is justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, and says he has been crucified with Christ, who now lives in him.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: Paul went up to Jerusalem after fourteen years with Barnabas and Titus by revelation, and laid the Good News he preaches among the Gentiles before the leaders. He refused to yield to the false brothers, received the right hand of fellowship from James, Cephas, and John, and resisted Peter to his face at Antioch. He declares that he has been crucified with Christ, that Christ lives in him, and that he lives by faith in the Son of God.

l: Peter, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: Peter is described as entrusted with the Good News for the circumcised, with God working through him in his apostleship. At Antioch he ate with the Gentiles until people came from James, then drew back and separated himself, fearing those of the circumcision. Paul resisted him to his face, saying he stood condemned.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: Jesus Christ is the one in whom believers seek to be justified, and Paul denies that this makes Christ a servant of sin. Paul says Christ lives in him, and that the Son of God loved him and gave himself up for him. If righteousness came through the law, Christ would have died for nothing.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: God worked through Peter in his apostleship to the circumcised and likewise through Paul among the Gentiles. The text states that God doesn't show partiality to man. Paul says he lives to God and does not reject God's grace.

l: Good News of Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: Paul preaches the Good News among the Gentiles and laid it before the Jerusalem leaders, who added nothing to him. He was entrusted with it for the uncircumcised, as Peter was for the circumcised. Paul did not yield to the false brothers so that the truth of the Good News might continue with the Galatians, and he says Peter and the others did not walk uprightly according to it.

l: Gentiles, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: Paul preaches the Good News among the Gentiles, and James, Cephas, and John agreed that he and Barnabas should go to them. Titus, a Greek, was not compelled to be circumcised. At Antioch Peter ate with Gentiles until he withdrew, and Paul asked why Peter compelled the Gentiles to live as Jews.

l: Jews, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: Paul says that he and Peter are Jews by nature and not Gentile sinners, yet they believed in Christ Jesus to be justified by faith and not by works of the law. At Antioch the rest of the Jews joined Peter in his hypocrisy. Paul accuses Peter of living as the Gentiles do while compelling Gentiles to live as the Jews do.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: The text states that no flesh will be justified by the works of the law, and that a man is justified through faith in Jesus Christ. Paul says he died to the law through the law so that he might live to God. He adds that if righteousness were through the law, Christ died for nothing, and that rebuilding what he destroyed would prove him a law-breaker.

l: justification by faith, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: Paul states that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, and that even he and Peter believed in Christ to be justified by faith. He denies that seeking justification in Christ makes Christ a servant of sin. He says that if righteousness were through the law, Christ died for nothing.

l: Peter's hypocrisy at Antioch, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 2
s: At Antioch Peter ate with the Gentiles before some people came from James, then drew back and separated himself, fearing those of the circumcision. The rest of the Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, and even Barnabas was carried away. Paul rebuked Peter before them all because they did not walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: In Galatians chapter 3 the writer rebukes the Galatians as foolish for turning from faith to the works of the law, asking whether they received the Spirit by works or by hearing with faith. He points to Abraham, who believed God and was counted righteous, to argue that those of faith are Abraham's children and are blessed with him. The law brings a curse on those who rely on its works, but Christ redeemed believers from that curse by becoming a curse for them, so that the blessing of Abraham and the promise of the Spirit might reach the Gentiles. The writer argues that the promise made to Abraham and his offspring, who is Christ, was confirmed by God and is not annulled by the law that came 430 years later. The law was added because of transgressions and served as a tutor until faith came, and now all who are in Christ are children of God, one in Christ, and Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise.

l: Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: The Galatians are called foolish and are asked whether they received the Spirit and saw miracles by works of the law or by hearing with faith. Having begun in the Spirit, they are questioned about being completed in the flesh, and they are told they are all children of God through faith in Christ Jesus, baptized into Christ, and, if Christ's, Abraham's offspring and heirs according to promise.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among the Galatians as crucified. He redeemed believers from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for them, and he is identified as the singular 'offspring' to whom the promise to Abraham was made.

l: Abraham, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness, and the Scripture preached the Good News to him beforehand, saying all nations would be blessed in him. Those who are of faith are called his children and are blessed with him, and God granted him the inheritance by promise.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: God justifies the Gentiles by faith and supplies the Spirit and works miracles among the Galatians. He confirmed the covenant with Abraham beforehand, granted the inheritance by promise, and is described as one, in contrast to a mediator.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: The law places those who rely on its works under a curse, is not of faith, and cannot justify anyone before God. It came 430 years after the promise without annulling it, was added because of transgressions and ordained through angels by a mediator, and served as a tutor to bring people to Christ until faith came.

l: faith, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: Faith is the means by which the Galatians received the Spirit and by which the righteous live. Those who are of faith are children of Abraham, are justified, and receive the promise of the Spirit; faith has now come, so believers are no longer under a tutor.

l: promise (to Abraham), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 3
s: The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his offspring, who is Christ, and the inheritance rests on promise rather than law. The law that came later does not annul it, and it is given by faith in Jesus Christ to those who believe, making believers heirs according to promise.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4 the author, writing to the brothers who desire to be under the law, explains that an heir who is a child is no different from a bondservant until the day appointed by the father. He says that when the fullness of time came, God sent his Son, born to a woman and under the law, to redeem those under the law so they might receive adoption as children, and sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts crying "Abba, Father!" He rebukes them for turning back to the weak and miserable elemental principles and observing days, months, seasons, and years, recalls how they once received him as an angel of God, and expresses his fear and perplexity about them. He then offers an allegory of Abraham's two sons, one by the servant Hagar, born according to the flesh, and one by the free woman, born through promise, representing two covenants and two Jerusalems. He concludes that the readers, like Isaac, are children of promise and not children of a servant, but of the free woman.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: God is said to have sent out his Son at the fullness of the time, born to a woman and under the law, to redeem those under the law. He also sent the Spirit of his Son into believers' hearts, making them sons and heirs through Christ, and the readers are described as now known by him.

l: Son of God (Christ Jesus), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: God sent out his Son, born to a woman and born under the law, so that he might redeem those under the law and bring about adoption as children. The author notes the readers once received him as an angel of God, even as Christ Jesus, and says he is in travail until Christ is formed in them.

l: Isaac, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: Isaac is named as the model for the readers: like him, they are children of promise. He is described as the one born according to the Spirit, who was persecuted by the one born according to the flesh, and the son of the free woman who will inherit.

l: Hagar, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: Hagar is identified in the allegory with the covenant from Mount Sinai, which bears children into bondage. She is said to be Mount Sinai in Arabia and to answer to the Jerusalem that exists now, being in bondage with her children.

l: free woman (Abraham's wife), Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The free woman bore Abraham's son through promise, in contrast to the servant's son born according to the flesh. The text quotes Scripture that the servant's son will not inherit with her son, and says the readers are children of the free woman, not of a servant.

l: Mount Sinai, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: Mount Sinai is the source of one of the two covenants, which bears children to bondage. The text equates Hagar with Mount Sinai in Arabia.

l: Jerusalem that exists now, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The Jerusalem that exists now is said to be answered to by Hagar/Mount Sinai. It is in bondage with her children.

l: Jerusalem that is above, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The Jerusalem that is above is described as free and as the mother of us all. It is linked to the quoted promise that the barren and desolate will have more children than the woman who has a husband.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The author speaks as one afraid that his labor for the readers may have been wasted, pleading with them to become as he is. He recalls preaching the Good News to them first because of weakness in his flesh, asks whether telling the truth has made him their enemy, says he is in travail again for them until Christ is formed in them, and wishes he could be present and change his tone because he is perplexed about them.

l: Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The readers are told that, as children, they are now sons and heirs of God through Christ, having received the Spirit crying "Abba, Father!" They are rebuked for turning back to the elemental principles and observing days, months, seasons, and years, though they once received the author as an angel of God and would have given him their eyes. They are called children of promise, like Isaac, and not children of a servant.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The law is what the Son was born under and what he came to redeem others from. Those who desire to be under it are asked whether they listen to it, since it records the account of Abraham's two sons that the author reads as an allegory.

l: elemental principles of the world, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The elemental principles of the world are the things under which the author and readers were held in bondage when they were children. The readers are asked why they turn back to these weak and miserable principles and desire bondage to them again, as shown by observing days, months, seasons, and years.

l: adoption as children, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: Adoption as children is the purpose for which the Son redeemed those under the law. Because the readers are children, God sent the Spirit of his Son into their hearts, so they are no longer bondservants but sons and heirs.

l: bondage, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: Bondage describes the condition of a child heir under guardians, of the author and readers under the elemental principles, and of the readers before they knew God, when they served those who are not gods. It is also the condition of Hagar's children and the present Jerusalem, and the readers are warned against desiring it all over again.

l: two covenants, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 4
s: The two covenants are presented as an allegory of the two sons of Abraham. One is from Mount Sinai and bears children to bondage, which is Hagar, while the other corresponds to the free woman, the Jerusalem above, and the children of promise.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: Paul urges his readers to stand firm in the liberty Christ gave them and warns that receiving circumcision cuts them off from Christ and obligates them to keep the whole law. He expresses confidence that they will not be swayed, says those who trouble them will bear judgment, and notes that his own persecution shows he does not preach circumcision. He explains that freedom is for serving one another through love, which fulfills the whole law, and warns against biting and devouring one another. He contrasts walking by the Spirit with the flesh, lists the deeds of the flesh and the fruit of the Spirit, and closes by saying those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh and should walk by the Spirit without conceit or envy.

l: Paul, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: Paul testifies that circumcision makes Christ profit his readers nothing, and he expresses confidence in them while saying their troubler will bear judgment. He argues that he is still persecuted because he does not preach circumcision, and he wishes the disturbers would cut themselves off. He urges the readers to walk by the Spirit and reminds them he forewarned them about the deeds of the flesh.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: Christ is said to have made believers free, and he will profit nothing those who receive circumcision. Those who seek justification by the law are alienated from him, and those who belong to him have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.

l: Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: The readers are urged to stand firm in their liberty and not be entangled again in a yoke of bondage. They were running well until someone interfered, and Paul is confident they will think no other way. They are called for freedom, told to serve one another in love, warned against biting and devouring each other, and urged to walk by the Spirit.

l: circumcision, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: Circumcision is presented as something that, if received, makes Christ profit nothing and makes a man a debtor to do the whole law. In Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision amounts to anything, and Paul says his not preaching it explains why the stumbling block of the cross has not been removed in his case.

l: the law, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: The law is something a man who receives circumcision is a debtor to keep entirely, and seeking justification by it means falling away from grace. The whole law is fulfilled in one word, loving one's neighbor as oneself, those led by the Spirit are not under it, and there is no law against the fruit of the Spirit.

l: liberty, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: Liberty is what Christ made believers free with, and they are told to stand firm in it. They were called for freedom but must not use it as an opportunity for the flesh; instead they use it to serve one another through love.

l: Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: Through the Spirit, by faith, believers wait for the hope of righteousness. The Spirit lusts against the flesh, those led by the Spirit are not under the law, and the fruit of the Spirit is described. Believers who live by the Spirit are told to walk by the Spirit.

l: the flesh, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: The flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the two are contrary to one another. Believers are told not to fulfill its lust and not to use freedom as an opportunity for it, and those who belong to Christ have crucified it with its passions and lusts.

l: deeds of the flesh, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: The deeds of the flesh are called obvious and are listed: adultery, sexual immorality, uncleanness, lustfulness, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, strife, jealousies, outbursts of anger, rivalries, divisions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, orgies, and similar things. Paul forewarns that those who practice such things will not inherit God's Kingdom.

l: fruit of the Spirit, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 5
s: The fruit of the Spirit is listed as love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. The text says there is no law against such things.

l: Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: In the closing chapter of the letter, the author instructs the brothers on how to live in community: restore a person caught in a fault gently, bear one another's burdens, examine one's own work, and support those who teach the word. He warns that God is not mocked and that what a man sows he will reap, with sowing to the flesh bringing corruption and sowing to the Spirit bringing eternal life, and urges them not to grow weary in doing good. Writing in large letters with his own hand, he accuses those who compel circumcision of seeking a good impression and avoiding persecution for the cross of Christ, and of wanting to boast in the recipients' flesh. He declares that he boasts only in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, that neither circumcision nor uncircumcision matters but a new creation, and that he bears the marks of Jesus on his body. He ends by blessing those who walk by this rule, and with a prayer for grace on the brothers.

l: Jesus Christ, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: Jesus Christ is called Lord, and keeping his law is described as bearing one another's burdens. His cross is the sole ground of the author's boasting, and the author bears his marks on his body. The letter closes with a prayer for his grace to be with the brothers' spirit.

l: God, Paul’s Letter to the Galatians, Chapter 6
s: God is said not to be mocked, because whatever a man sows he will also reap. The text also speaks of "God's Israel" as those on whom peace and mercy are pronounced for walking by the rule that circumcision and uncircumcision count for nothing but a new creation does.
